newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Burns Philp shareholders irate at AGM.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Burns Philp shareholders irate at AGM.

text.p: Irate Burns Philp and Co Ltd shareholders on Monday refused to rubber stamp the re-election of a director at an annual general meeting that was peppered with criticism of the company's performance.
Shareholders at the three-hour meeting attacked the company's poor results, non-payment of a final dividend and "bucketfuls of promises of improved performance".
Andrew Little, a small shareholder, told the meeting the company had "sold good assets and purchased rubbishy ones".
He later opposed the re-election of Alan McGregor, chairman of F.H. Faulding & Co Ltd and James Hardie Industries Ltd, saying Burns Philp needed marketing experience rather than lawyers.
McGregor's re-election was defeated on a show of hands.
Acting chairman William Irvine called for a poll but acknowledged to shareholders that McGregor would be re-elected with the overwhelming support of proxy votes.
Another director Mark Burrows had earlier been voted back by 85 votes to 63 on a show of hands.
Burns Philp reported a 42 percent rise in net profit for the first quarter to September 30 to A$17.6 million after reporting a net loss of A$61.8 million for the 1995/96 year to June 30.
Asked about the shareholder reaction after the meeting, managing director Ian Clack told reporters he was little surprised.
"I think the majority of the shareholders here were probably more upset about the cut to the final dividend," he said.
"They are relatively small shareholders and a lot of them are relying on the dividend for their economic sustenance."
Clack said he expected the company to improve its performance over the year, but said it was too early to put a number to the improvement.
Raw material costs were falling, while slotting fees, which are paid to ensure supermaket display space, were abating.
He said the level of competition was starting to ease in the U.S. spice market where Burns Philp is in competition with the world's number one spices firm McCormick and Co Inc.
"We would hope to see that continue," he said. "We have one major competitor and their stockholders are about as happy as ours because their margins went down the same way ours did."
However, Clack said it could take three or four years for Burns Philp to reach its target of a 15 per cent return on assets, which came in at 6.3 per cent in 1996.
He also said the stronger Australian dollar would have a "net adverse effect" on profits.
The Australian dollar was currently around US$0.79 against US$0.75 in the first half of last year, which would translate into a six percent reduction of Australian dollar profits, he said.
